subject: English
chapter: First Flight: A Letter to God
text: Lencho, a hardworking farmer, grows corn and depends on a good harvest. A hailstorm destroys his crop. He writes a letter to God asking for 100 pesos. The postmaster, moved by Lencho faith, collects 70 pesos from postal employees and sends it in God name. Lencho opens the letter, finds only 70 pesos, and writes again to God complaining that the post office employees must have stolen the rest. Theme: Lencho unshakeable faith in God contrasts with distrust of fellow human beings. The postmaster represents human goodness and compassion. Irony: the very people who helped him are suspected of theft.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight: Nelson Mandela - Long Walk to Freedom
text: Extract from Mandela autobiography describing his inauguration on 10 May 1994 as South Africa first Black President. Military generals who once imprisoned him now salute him. He reflects on how South Africa transformed from racial apartheid to democracy. Mandela speaks of two obligations: to family and to his people. He describes courage as being both fearful and brave. The long walk to freedom must continue as every person is born free. Theme: freedom, courage, racial equality, dignity, transformation. Apartheid: South African policy of racial segregation denying Black people basic rights, dismantled through decades of struggle.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight: Two Stories about Flying
text: His First Flight (Liam O Flaherty): young seagull afraid to make his first flight. Siblings and parents have flown. Mother tempts him with a fish. Driven by hunger he dives and finds himself flying. Theme: overcoming fear and taking first step towards independence. Black Aeroplane (Frederick Forsyth): pilot flying through storm over France encounters mysterious black aeroplane with no lights that guides him to safety. No record of other plane exists when he lands. Theme: mystery, gratitude, questions about reality. Help from unknown sources.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight: From the Diary of Anne Frank
text: Anne Frank, Jewish girl hiding from Nazis during World War II, writes in her diary about loneliness that led her to keep a diary (paper has more patience than people). She contrasts distant relationship with her mother against an ideal relationship. Describes classmates at school before going into hiding. Anne hopes her diary will be a true friend for life. Historical context: Anne Frank family hid in secret annexe in Amsterdam 1942-1944. Discovered, arrested, sent to concentration camps. Anne died in Bergen-Belsen camp in 1945 just weeks before liberation. Father Otto Frank survived and published her diary. Themes: loneliness, friendship, hope, war impact on children.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight: The Sermon at Benares
text: Siddhartha Gautama born into royal family 563 BCE. At age 25 he saw four sights: old man, sick man, funeral procession, and monk. Renounced worldly life. After 7 years of searching attained enlightenment under Bodhi tree at age 35, became the Buddha. Gave first sermon at Benares (Varanasi). Kisa Gotami: lost her child, went mad with grief. Buddha asked her to bring mustard seeds from a house where no one had died. She found no such house, realised death is universal, and accepted her grief. Theme: death is universal and part of all human life; acceptance brings peace. Illustrates Buddhist concept of the Four Noble Truths.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight: The Proposal - Anton Chekhov
text: One-act comedy. Characters: Lomov (nervous, weak landowner), Natalya (stubborn, argumentative), Chubukov (her father, eager for her marriage). Lomov visits to propose but before proposing mentions his land Oxen Meadows. Natalya claims it belongs to her family. They quarrel fiercely. Lomov has palpitations and leaves. Realising his purpose was marriage, Natalya becomes eager. Father forces Lomov to propose. Just as proposal is made they argue again about whose dog is better. Chubukov hastily marries them. Theme: satire on aristocratic society, trivial disputes, greed for land and status, selfishness disguised as love. Humour comes from irony that important matters (love) are abandoned for trivial arguments.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight Poems: Dust of Snow, Fire and Ice
text: Dust of Snow (Robert Frost): crow shakes snow off hemlock tree onto poet; this small moment changes the poet mood from regret to better mood. Crow (bad omen) and hemlock (poisonous tree) are agents of good mood change. Theme: small moments of nature can powerfully affect our state of mind; good can come from seemingly negative things. Fire and Ice (Robert Frost): poet reflects on two ways world could end - fire (symbolising desire or passion) or ice (symbolising hatred or indifference). Both lead to destruction. Theme: human emotions - desire and hatred - are capable of destroying the world. Short poem with deep philosophical meaning about human destructive nature.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight Poems: A Tiger in the Zoo, How to Tell Wild Animals
text: A Tiger in the Zoo (Leslie Norris): contrasts tiger in zoo with tiger in the wild. In zoo tiger paces in velvet quiet rage, ignores visitors. In wild he would be near water hole terrorising the village. Theme: captivity versus freedom; animals deserve to live freely; zoo life is unnatural and cruel. How to Tell Wild Animals (Carolyn Wells): humorous poem about identifying wild animals. If a beast charges and tears you it is an Asian lion. Bengal tiger will eat you with a peculiar smile. Crocodile weeps while eating you (false tears). Theme: ironic humour; the advice is useless as identifying the animal means you have already been killed.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight Poems: The Ball Poem, Amanda
text: The Ball Poem (John Berryman): boy loses his ball in harbour and is inconsolable. Poet thinks how boy must learn that loss is part of life. Ball represents childhood, innocence, first possessions. Boy learns epistemology of loss: things are lost and cannot be retrieved with money. Theme: loss, learning to deal with it, growing up. Amanda (Robin Klein): child Amanda is constantly nagged about posture, homework, eating, cleaning. Meanwhile she daydreams of being a mermaid, Rapunzel, or a free orphan. Theme: contrast between parental control and child need for freedom; children create inner worlds to escape constant nagging; irony that mother may have good intentions but suffocates the child.

subject: English
text: Mrs Pumphrey pampers her dog Tricki with too much food and no exercise. Tricki becomes obese, listless, and unwell. Vet Mr Herriot persuades Mrs Pumphrey to hospitalise the dog. At the surgery Tricki is given no food for two days, just water, then begins to eat well, plays with other dogs, and becomes healthy. After two weeks Tricki is returned. Mrs Pumphrey calls it a triumph of surgery. Vet privately admits it was a triumph of letting nature take over. Theme: over-pampering can be harmful; moderation is important; excess love without discipline can be destructive. Gentle satire on excessive sentimentality of wealthy pet owners.

subject: English
text: Hari Singh, a young thief, befriends Anil, a kind and trusting writer, and works for him as a cook. Hari plans to rob Anil and one night steals his money. At the railway station he hesitates thinking about how Anil, who was teaching him to read and write, will no longer trust him and the opportunity for a new life will be lost. He returns the money before Anil notices. Anil gives him money with a smile suggesting he suspects but forgives. Theme: trust and friendship can transform a person; possibility of redemption; value of education and honest life over material gain. Hari Singh character arc shows moral development.

subject: English
text: Griffin is a brilliant scientist who discovered how to make his body invisible by swallowing certain drugs. He is lawless and becomes a vagabond. Commits arson against his landlord and steals. His footprints are noticed in London mud. He wraps himself in bandages and dark glasses in Iping village. Steals from a clergyman. Villagers discover his secret. He reveals himself and escapes. Theme: science without ethics and morality is dangerous; irresponsibility and misuse of scientific knowledge leads to self-destruction. Griffin represents the scientist-villain archetype. Invisibility without moral restraint leads to crime and eventual ruin.

subject: English
text: Matilda Loisel is a pretty woman married to a minor government clerk but dreams of luxury. Her husband gets invitation to a grand ball. She borrows a diamond necklace from her wealthy friend Madame Forestier. At the ball she is a great success. On returning home she discovers the necklace is lost. They borrow 36000 francs and buy an identical diamond necklace. They spend 10 years in poverty paying off the debt. When she meets Madame Forestier who does not recognise her and tells her story, Madame Forestier reveals the original necklace was fake - worth only 500 francs. Theme: false pride, vanity, and materialism lead to ruin; appearance versus reality; one moment of pretension can destroy a whole life.

subject: English
text: Bholi (Sulekha) is a simple girl who dropped on her head as a baby and developed a slight stutter and was disfigured by smallpox. Her family considers her a burden. When school opens she is sent there. Her teacher Miss Lakshmi is kind and encourages Bholi with affection. Bholi blossoms into a confident, literate woman. When a greedy old man agrees to marry her without dowry, he demands a large sum at the last minute at the ceremony. Bholi boldly refuses to marry him and decides to become a teacher like Miss Lakshmi. Theme: education transforms lives; importance of a good teacher; women should stand up against exploitation; looks do not define a person worth.

subject: English
text: Reported Speech rules: remove inverted commas; use that for statements. Change tenses (backshift): is/am->was; are->were; has/have->had; will->would; can->could; may->might; shall->should. Change time expressions: now->then; today->that day; yesterday->the day before; tomorrow->the next day; here->there; this->that. For questions: use if/whether for yes-no questions; use question word for wh-questions; change to statement word order. For commands: use to+infinitive or not to+infinitive for negative. Tenses: Present Simple (habitual/facts), Present Continuous (ongoing), Present Perfect (recent with present relevance), Past Simple (completed), Past Perfect (before another past action), Future Simple (will/shall).

subject: English
text: Active voice: subject performs the action. The dog bit the man. Passive voice: subject receives the action. The man was bitten by the dog. Formation: object of active becomes subject of passive; use be + past participle; subject of active becomes agent in by phrase (often omitted). Tense changes: Simple Present -> is/am/are + past participle; Simple Past -> was/were + past participle; Present Perfect -> has/have been + past participle; Future -> will be + past participle; Present Continuous -> is/am/are being + past participle. Use passive when agent is unknown, unimportant, or obvious; in formal and scientific writing. Modal passives: can/should/must + be + past participle.
